Gaussian Triangle Rendering is a surface reconstruction technique that represents primitives as "Gaussian triangles"—composed of three 2D Gaussian ellipses connected by common tangent lines—to achieve better surface continuity than single ellipses [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Gaussian Triangle Rendering represents primitives as 'Gaussian triangles' composed of three 2D Gaussian ellipses connected by common tangent lines to achieve better surface continuity. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines 'Gaussian triangles' as triangle-centered primitives. It details the process of decomposing the triangle into three vertices, splatting them as point-based (Gaussian) ellipses, and then deriving 'common tangent lines' between these boundary ellipses to form the edges of the triangle (Steps 1-3). The evidence further explains that this method handles 'inner', 'vertex', and 'edge' regions separately to define the fading parameter, which ensures smooth transitions (better surface continuity) compared to standard methods. Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
